The formula is false. There is a family of counterexamples with
$$k=m,\qquad SF_2(F)=4,\qquad \beta_2(G)=2m+4,\qquad SF_2(G)=3m
\quad(m\ge5).$$
Thus, for  $m=5$ , the exact separation is
$$\boxed{SF_2(G)=15>14=2k+SF_2(F)=\beta_2(G).}$$
The failure comes from selecting opposite vertices in each square: the selected root can depend on a vertex of  $F$  for its activity, giving that vertex a deletion witness which disappears when the roots are removed.1. Explicit constructionFix  $m\ge5$ . Let
$$T=\{t_1,\ldots,t_m\},\qquad X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\},$$
and introduce distinct roots  $d_i,e_i$  for  $1\le i\le m$ .Define the base graph  $B$  by exactly the following edges:All edges within  $T$ , making  $T$  a clique.All edges within  $X$ , making  $X$  a clique.The three edges
$$d_ie_i,\qquad d_it_i,\qquad d_ix_i$$
for each  $i$ .There are no other base edges. Take the matching
$$E_0=\{d_ie_i:1\le i\le m\}.$$
Then  $k=m$ , and deleting all its endpoints gives
$$F=B-\{d_i,e_i:1\le i\le m\}=K_m\sqcup K_m.$$
Now perform exactly the prescribed attachments: introduce  $a_i,b_i$  and add
$$d_ia_i,\qquad a_ib_i,\qquad b_ie_i.$$
Every quadruple  $\{d_i,a_i,b_i,e_i\}$  induces the required square.For clarity, the complete neighborhoods in  $G$  are:VertexNeighborhood $t_i$  $(T\setminus\{t_i\})\cup\{d_i\}$  $x_i$  $(X\setminus\{x_i\})\cup\{d_i\}$  $d_i$  $\{e_i,a_i,t_i,x_i\}$  $e_i$  $\{d_i,b_i\}$  $a_i$  $\{d_i,b_i\}$  $b_i$  $\{a_i,e_i\}$ For  $m=5$ ,  $B$  has  $20$  vertices and  $G$  has  $30$  vertices.2. Computing  $SF_2(F)$ In a clique  $K_m$ , with  $m\ge2$ , the inclusion-minimal forming sets are exactly its two-element subsets:The empty set is not forming.A singleton is not forming: every outside vertex has just one selected neighbor, and that selected vertex is inactive.Any pair is forming, since every outside vertex has two selected neighbors.Any larger set contains a forming pair and therefore is not minimal.Formation and minimality separate over connected components. Hence
$$\boxed{SF_2(F)=SF_2(K_m)+SF_2(K_m)=4.}$$
Likewise, a dissociation set contains at most two vertices from each clique, so
$$\beta_2(F)=4.$$
3. A minimal forming set of size  $3m$ Set
$$S=T\cup\{d_i,b_i:1\le i\le m\}.$$
Thus
$$|S|=3m.$$
The selected graph  $G[S]$  consists of the clique  $T$ , a selected vertex  $d_i$  adjacent only to  $t_i$  for each  $i$ , and the isolated selected vertices  $b_i$ . In particular, every  $d_i$  is active because  $t_i$  is selected.FormationThe outside vertices are exactly the  $x_i,a_i,e_i$ .Each  $a_i$  has the two selected neighbors  $d_i,b_i$ .Each  $e_i$  has the two selected neighbors  $d_i,b_i$ .Each  $x_i$  has the selected neighbor  $d_i$ , which is active through the selected edge  $d_it_i$ .Therefore  $S$  is forming.Every deletion failsHere are witnesses for every selected vertex, for every  $i$ :Deleted vertexWitness outside the reduced setWhy the witness is unformed $t_i$  $x_i$ Its only selected neighbor is  $d_i$ . After deleting  $t_i$ ,  $d_i$  has no selected neighbor and is inactive. $d_i$  $a_i$ Its only selected neighbor is  $b_i$ , which is inactive because both  $a_i,e_i$  are outside. $b_i$  $b_i$  itselfBoth its neighbors  $a_i,e_i$  are outside, so it has no selected neighbor.The first row follows directly from
$$N_G(d_i)=\{e_i,a_i,t_i,x_i\}:$$
before the deletion, only  $t_i$  among these is selected.Formation is upward closed: adding selected vertices cannot remove selected neighbors or deactivate a selected vertex. Consequently, failure of every single-vertex deletion proves inclusion-minimality.Thus
$$SF_2(G)\ge3m.$$
Since  $m\ge5$ ,
$$3m>2m+4=2k+SF_2(F).$$
This already supplies a complete counterexample with all minimality witnesses.4. Exact upper bound:  $SF_2(G)=3m$ We can also determine  $SF_2(G)$  exactly. First, here is a check of the local square fact used in the argument.Local square lemmaFor an attachment
$$d-a-b-e-d,$$
every minimal forming set contains exactly two vertices of the square.At least two are necessary. With no selected square vertex, a new vertex has no selected neighbor. With exactly one selected root, the new vertex opposite it has no selected neighbor. With exactly one selected new vertex, that vertex is inactive, and the other new vertex has it as its sole selected neighbor.Three or four allow a safe deletion. Up to the symmetry exchanging  $d,e$  and  $a,b$ , the cases are:If  $\{d,e,a\}$  is selected, delete  $a$ . The remaining selected edge  $de$  forms both new vertices. The only remaining selected neighbor of  $a$  is  $d$ , whose activity persists through  $e$ .If  $\{d,a,b\}$  is selected, delete  $b$ . The remaining selected edge  $da$  forms both newly outside  $b$  and omitted root  $e$ . The remaining selected neighbor  $a$  stays active.If all four are selected, delete  $a$ . The newly outside  $a$  has two selected neighbors  $d,b$ , and both  $d,b$  remain active through  $e$ .In each case, the deleted new vertex has no neighbors outside its square, and every remaining selected neighbor of it stays active. Thus no other outside vertex loses formation. These are valid safe deletions even with arbitrary base edges incident to the roots.Also, any two selected square vertices form the two omitted square vertices using only the square: an adjacent pair is active, while an opposite pair gives each omitted vertex two selected neighbors.Bounding the selected vertices in  $F$ Let  $R$  be any minimal forming set of our constructed  $G$ , and write
$$p=|R\cap T|,\qquad q=|R\cap X|.$$
The local lemma gives
$$|R|=2m+p+q.$$
We claim
$$p\ge3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad q=0.$$
Suppose instead that  $p\ge3$  and  $q\ge1$ . Choose a selected  $t_i$ , and put
$$R'=R\setminus\{t_i\}.$$
We show that  $R'$  is still forming.Square vertices. Each square retains its two selected vertices. Every outside square vertex is therefore still formed locally.Vertices of  $T$ , including the deleted  $t_i$ . There are  $p-1\ge2$  remaining selected vertices in  $T$ . Every outside vertex of  $T$  is adjacent to all of them.Vertices of  $X$ . Their selected-neighbor sets do not change, because there are no  $T$ - $X$  edges. The activity of a selected  $X$ -vertex also cannot change when  $t_i$  is deleted.The only selected vertex outside  $T$  whose activity could be lost is  $d_i$ . Among vertices of  $X$ , this could affect only  $x_i$ . But if  $x_i$  is outside and  $d_i$  is selected, then  $x_i$  has both:the selected neighbor  $d_i$ , anda selected neighbor in  $X$ , since  $q\ge1$ .Thus  $x_i$  still has two selected neighbors, regardless of whether  $d_i$  remains active. All other outside  $X$ -vertices retain their formation.Hence  $R'$  is forming, contradicting minimality. This proves the claim. By symmetry,
$$q\ge3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad p=0.$$
It follows that either one clique contributes no selected vertices, giving
$$p+q\le m,$$
or both contribute at most two, giving
$$p+q\le4.$$
Since  $m\ge5$ , in either case  $p+q\le m$ . Therefore
$$|R|\le2m+m=3m.$$
Combined with the explicit minimal set above,
$$\boxed{SF_2(G)=3m.}$$
5. Exact dissociation separationThe dissociation calculation also holds exactly.A dissociation set uses at most two vertices from each square: every three-vertex subset of an induced  $C_4$  contains a vertex of induced degree two. It also uses at most two vertices from each of the cliques  $T,X$ . Consequently,
$$\beta_2(G)\le2m+4.$$
Equality is attained by selecting all new pairs  $a_i,b_i$ , together with two vertices from each of  $T$  and  $X$ . The selected induced graph is a disjoint union of  $m+2$  edges. Hence
$$\boxed{\beta_2(G)=2m+4.}$$
For  $m=5$ , all relevant values are therefore exact:
$$\boxed{
SF_2(F)=\beta_2(F)=4,\qquad
\beta_2(G)=14,\qquad
SF_2(G)=15.
}$$
6. The precise failure of the proposed upper boundIn the exhibited minimal set, every square selects the opposite pair
$$\{d_i,b_i\}.$$
This pair forms the omitted square vertices, but it supplies no selected neighbor to  $d_i$ . The root’s activity instead depends uniquely on  $t_i$ .The outside vertex  $x_i$  is formed through the selected edge  $d_it_i$ . Deleting  $t_i$  deactivates  $d_i$ , leaving  $x_i$  with exactly one selected neighbor, now inactive. Thus  $x_i$  makes  $t_i$  indispensable.This makes every vertex of the entire clique  $T$  indispensable in  $G$ , even though only two vertices of that clique can belong to a minimal forming set of  $F$ .Indeed,
$$S\cap V(F)=T$$
does not form  $F$ , because it selects nothing in  $X$ . Moreover, no extension of  $T$  inside  $F$  can be minimal forming: such an extension must select at least two vertices in  $X$ , after which deleting any  $t_i$  still leaves at least two selected vertices in  $T$ .The two-selected-vertices-per-square fact remains valid. What fails is the attempted bound on the number selected in  $F$ : roots can create activity-dependent deletion witnesses that do not exist in  $F$ . The resulting discrepancy is unbounded:
$$\boxed{
SF_2(G)-\bigl(2k+SF_2(F)\bigr)=m-4
\qquad(m\ge5).
}$$

restricted_median_question.response:
Unresolved. I have neither a proof of the universal degree-four statement nor a counterexample satisfying all of your restrictions. The searches did not produce a qualifying counterexample, and I do not use their finite outcomes as premises.There are, however, three rigorous reductions worth retaining:The entire two-connected maximum-degree-three case satisfies equality.In a planar median graph of maximum degree four, every connected collection of intersecting cubes is an induced convex chain
$$C_4\square P_k.$$
Branching and cyclic arrangements of cubes are impossible.A square attached along an edge gives an exact restriction on every minimal forming set. This settles an infinite family within your degree-four class that has no adjacent involutory automorphism.I give the proofs, then identify the remaining obstruction.1. The maximum-degree-three case is completely settledProposition 1Every finite two-connected median graph  $G$  with  $\Delta(G)\le 3$  is either
$$P_t\square K_2\qquad(t\ge2)$$
or  $Q_3$ . Consequently,
$$SF_2(P_t\square K_2)=\beta_2(P_t\square K_2)
 =2\left\lceil\frac t2\right\rceil,
\qquad
SF_2(Q_3)=\beta_2(Q_3)=4.$$
ProofIf  $G$  contains an induced cube, every vertex of that cube already has three neighbours inside it. The degree bound forbids an edge from the cube to its complement. Connectedness therefore gives  $G=Q_3$ .Suppose  $G$  has no induced cube. We use the following exact characterization of Bandelt–Chepoi–Eppstein: a finite median graph admits a squaregraph embedding precisely when it contains no induced cube, no induced book  $K_2\square K_{1,3}$ , and no induced suspended cogwheel. Here a squaregraph embedding has quadrilateral bounded faces and interior vertices of degree at least four. The book has maximum degree four; a suspended cogwheel has a hub of degree at least five. Thus the degree-three bound excludes both remaining obstructions, and  $G$  admits a squaregraph embedding. This is Proposition 9 of their author manuscript, with the suspended-cogwheel definition immediately preceding it. pageperso.lis-lab.frThere are no interior vertices in this embedding, because each would have degree at least four. Two-connectivity makes the outer-face boundary a simple cycle containing every vertex. The other edges are noncrossing chords, and the bounded faces are quadrilaterals.The weak dual of this polygonal quadrangulation is a tree: the bounded faces are connected through shared chords, and each chord separates the polygon, so its dual edge is a bridge.Every primal vertex already has its two outer-boundary edges. It can therefore belong to at most one chord. Consequently, a quadrilateral has at most two shared edges; if it has two, they are opposite. Its weak-dual vertex thus has degree at most two.The weak dual is a path. Restoring its faces successively constructs a chain of squares, with opposite attachment edges in every internal square. This is exactly a ladder  $P_t\square K_2$ .The parameter equalities follow from the bipartite prism theorem supplied in the question, using
$$\alpha(P_t)=\left\lceil\frac t2\right\rceil
\quad\text{and}\quad
Q_3=C_4\square K_2.$$
∎In fact, the classification proof does not need planarity as an initial hypothesis: the squaregraph characterization supplies it.Thus any counterexample to your question must have an actual degree-four vertex.2. At degree four, intersecting cubes form convex chainsThis reduction uses both planarity and the degree bound in a substantial way.Proposition 2Let  $G$  be a finite planar median graph with  $\Delta(G)\le4$ . Define  $\mathcal C(G)$  to have one vertex for each induced  $Q_3$  in  $G$ , with two cubes adjacent when their vertex sets intersect.Every connected component of  $\mathcal C(G)$  is a path. If it contains  $r\ge1$  cubes, their union is an induced convex subgraph
$$T\cong C_4\square P_{r+1}.$$
Moreover:Every vertex in an internal  $C_4$  layer has degree four in  $G$ .All edges between  $T$  and  $G-V(T)$  meet its two end layers.There are at most eight such edges.If  $r\ge2$ , every connected component of  $G-V(T)$  attaches entirely to one end layer.Two-connectivity is not needed for this proposition.Preliminary median factsI record the needed facts directly.Median graphs are bipartite. Fix a root  $o$ . If adjacent vertices  $u,v$  had equal distance from  $o$ , the median of  $o,u,v$  would have to be an endpoint of
$$I(u,v)=\{u,v\}.$$
Neither endpoint lies in the required interval from  $o$  to the other endpoint. This is impossible. Adjacent vertices therefore have distances from  $o$  differing by one, giving a bipartition by distance parity.Two distinct vertices have at most two common neighbours. If  $a,c$  had three common neighbours  $b,d,e$ , the latter three vertices would have pairwise distance two. Both  $a$  and  $c$  would belong to their three pairwise intervals, contradicting uniqueness of their median.Every four-cycle is convex. Its opposite vertices have exactly its two intervening vertices as common neighbours. Thus all shortest paths between opposite vertices remain in the square. The other pairs are adjacent.Every induced cube is convex. First, it is isometric: cube-distance-two pairs remain at distance two, and antipodal pairs remain at distance three, by bipartiteness and inducedness.Only antipodal pairs need further consideration. Let  $u,v$  be antipodal cube vertices, and suppose an outside vertex  $z$  lies on a shortest  $u$ - $v$  path. After interchanging  $u,v$ , assume
$$d(u,z)=1,\qquad d(z,v)=2.$$
Choose a cube neighbour  $a$  of  $u$ . Then
$$d(z,a)=d(a,v)=d(z,v)=2.$$
The median  $m$  of  $z,a,v$  must be adjacent to all three.Since  $I(a,v)$  is a convex square inside the cube,  $m$  is a cube vertex at distance two from  $u$ . But  $z$  is then an outside common neighbour of  $u,m$ , contradicting convexity of the cube square having  $u,m$  as opposite vertices.Finally, a cube subgraph cannot have an additional antipodal edge: such an edge would create a third common neighbour for a distance-two pair. Thus considering induced cubes loses no cube configurations.Step 1: two intersecting cubes share a squareIntersections of convex vertex sets are convex. A nonempty convex subset of a hypercube is a coordinate face: relative to a chosen base vertex, interval closure supplies every combination of the coordinates that vary in the subset.Suppose distinct cubes  $C,D$  intersect in a face of dimension  $d$ . At any vertex  $v$  of their intersection, each cube contributes three incident edges and precisely  $d$  of those edges are shared. Hence
$$\deg_G(v)\ge 6-d.$$
The degree bound gives  $d\ge2$ , while distinctness gives  $d\le2$ . Therefore
$$C\cap D\cong C_4.$$
In particular, cubes cannot meet only at a vertex or an edge.Step 2: a cube meets other cubes only on opposite facesAt most one other cube can meet a fixed cube  $C$  on a given face  $F$ . Once a cube  $D$  is attached there, every vertex of  $F$  has:two neighbours in  $F$ ;one neighbour in  $C-F$ ;one neighbour in  $D-F$ .Degree four is exhausted. Any further cube attached to  $F$  must use the same off-face neighbours and hence is  $D$ .Now suppose cubes  $D,E$  meet  $C$  on adjacent faces. Let the common edge of these faces be  $ab$ . At  $a$ , the extra neighbour supplied by  $D$  must coincide with that supplied by  $E$ , because  $C$  already supplies three neighbours. Denote it by  $a'$ ; similarly obtain  $b'$ .The vertices
$$a,b,b',a'$$
form a common square of  $D,E$ . By Step 1 this is exactly  $D\cap E$ , and the triple intersection  $C\cap D\cap E$  is exactly  $ab$ .The union of these three cubes has
$$|V|=3\cdot8-3\cdot4+2=14,$$
and
$$|E|=3\cdot12-3\cdot4+1=25.$$
But a simple planar bipartite graph on fourteen vertices has at most
$$2\cdot14-4=24$$
edges. Contradiction.Thus the attachment faces of other cubes to  $C$  are pairwise opposite. There are at most two.Step 3: cycles of cubes are impossibleThe intersection graph  $\mathcal C(G)$  has maximum degree two. Its finite components are paths or cycles.Suppose one component is a cycle of  $r\ge3$  cubes. Each cube meets its two neighbours in opposite, disjoint square faces. There are no triple intersections. The union consequently has
$$|V|=8r-4r=4r,\qquad
|E|=12r-4r=8r.$$
The planar bipartite bound would require
$$8r\le 2(4r)-4,$$
which is impossible.Every component is therefore a path.Step 4: the resulting chain is inducedAlong a path of cubes, the two shared faces of every internal cube are opposite. Relabelling consecutive square layers removes any choice of square automorphism in the identifications. The edge-union is therefore
$$T=C_4\square P_{r+1}.$$
It has
$$|V(T)|=4r+4,\qquad
|E(T)|=8r+4=2|V(T)|-4.$$
An additional edge of  $G$  between vertices of  $T$  would violate the planar bipartite edge bound on that vertex set. Thus  $T$  is induced.Step 5: the entire chain is convexUse the embedding of  $T$  inherited from  $G$ . The graph  $T$  is two-connected and bipartite, so its facial boundaries are cycles of length at least four. Equality
$$|E(T)|=2|V(T)|-4$$
in Euler’s bound forces every facial boundary to be a four-cycle.Every component of  $G-V(T)$ , together with the interiors of its attachment edges, lies within a single face of  $T$ .Suppose a geodesic between vertices of  $T$  leaves  $T$ . Take one excursion whose endpoints  $x,y$  belong to  $T$  and whose internal vertices lie outside  $T$ . Those internal vertices lie in one outside component, so  $x,y$  belong to the four-cycle bounding its face.The excursion is a shortest  $x$ - $y$  path leaving that four-cycle. This contradicts the convexity of every four-cycle proved above. Hence  $T$  is convex.Step 6: only the end layers can meet the rest of the graphAn internal-layer vertex has two neighbours around its  $C_4$  and two longitudinal neighbours. Its degree is already four. An end-layer vertex has degree three inside  $T$ , leaving room for at most one external edge.There are eight end-layer vertices, giving at most eight external edges.For  $r\ge2$ , all neighbours in  $T$  of a given outside component lie on one facial four-cycle. Every four-cycle of
$$C_4\square P_{r+1}$$
is either a single layer or a Cartesian square in two consecutive layers. Neither can contain vertices of both end layers when  $r\ge2$ . Since internal vertices are saturated, that outside component attaches entirely to one end.If  $G$  is two-connected, each nonempty outside component must have at least two distinct attachment vertices; otherwise its sole attachment would be a cut vertex. ∎What this settles about cubesAn isolated chain is already covered by the supplied prism theorem:
$$C_4\square P_{r+1}
\cong (K_2\square P_{r+1})\square K_2.$$
Since  $\alpha(K_2\square P_{r+1})=r+1$ ,
$$SF_2(T)=\beta_2(T)=2(r+1)=\frac{|V(T)|}{2}.$$
The remaining cube issue is therefore specifically about attachments to these chains, rather than arbitrary arrangements of cubes.3. An exact square restriction, and a degree-four family it settlesThe following lemma concerns the parameters themselves.Lemma 3Suppose  $G$  contains the square
$$C=u-a-b-v-u,
\qquad \deg_G(a)=\deg_G(b)=2.$$
Then every inclusion-minimal forming set  $S$  satisfies
$$\boxed{|S\cap V(C)|=2,}$$
and
$$\boxed{\beta_2(G)=2+\beta_2(G-V(C)).}$$
No median or planarity assumption is needed.Proof of the forming-set assertionA forming set must select at least two vertices of  $C$ .If its sole selected vertex were  $u$ , then  $b$  would have no selected neighbour; the case of  $v$  is symmetric. If its sole selected vertex were  $a$ , then  $b$  would have only the selected neighbour  $a$ , which is inactive because both neighbours of  $a$  are unselected. The case of  $b$  is symmetric. Zero selections also fail.Now suppose exactly three vertices of  $C$  are selected. They form a selected  $P_3$ , and at least one endpoint of that path is  $a$  or  $b$ . Delete such an endpoint.The newly deleted vertex sees the middle vertex, which remains active through the other endpoint.The previously unselected square vertex retains an active selected neighbour.Every remaining selected vertex of the square lies on the remaining selected edge.No vertex outside the square loses a selected neighbour, because the deleted vertex has degree two.Thus formation survives, contradicting minimality.If all four are selected, delete  $a$ . The newly deleted  $a$  has the two selected neighbours  $u,b$ , and both  $u,b$  remain active through  $v$ . Again formation survives.Therefore every minimal forming set selects exactly two vertices of  $C$ . This proof explicitly checks the newly deleted vertex.For the dissociation identity, any induced degree-at-most-one set contains at most two vertices of a four-cycle, so
$$\beta_2(G)\le2+\beta_2(G-V(C)).$$
Conversely, any dissociation set in  $G-V(C)$  extends by  $\{a,b\}$ : these form an isolated selected edge, since their other neighbours  $u,v$  have been omitted. ∎Simultaneous versionLet  $C_1,\dots,C_k$  be vertex-disjoint squares of this form, and put
$$R=V(G)\setminus\bigcup_{i=1}^kV(C_i).$$
Then, for every minimal forming set  $S$ ,
$$|S|=2k+|S\cap R|,$$
while
$$\beta_2(G)=2k+\beta_2(G[R]).$$
In particular, equality follows whenever  $\Delta(G[R])\le1$ . If the squares partition all vertices, every minimal forming set has exactly half the vertices.An infinite family satisfying all your restrictionsFor even  $n\ge4$ , start with the ladder  $P_n\square K_2$ , with vertices
$$(i,j),\qquad i\in\{0,1\},\quad 0\le j<n.$$
For each row  $i$  and each  $0\le j<n/2$ , write
$$u=(i,2j),\qquad v=(i,2j+1),$$
and add two new vertices  $a_{ij},b_{ij}$  and exactly the three edges
$$u a_{ij},\qquad a_{ij}b_{ij},\qquad b_{ij}v.$$

$$\boxed{SF_2(G)=\beta_2(G)=2n.}$$

Adding a path between the endpoints of an existing edge preserves two-connectivity. Deleting either endpoint leaves the new path attached at the other endpoint; deleting a new vertex leaves its surviving segment attached to the old graph.Planarity. $$d_G(a,x)=1+d_H(u,x),\qquad
d_G(b,x)=1+d_H(v,x).$$
